panels.description: Wide, full page width. The mandapa of Padmanabhaswamy at night. Oil lamps in brass holders burn along every wall and pillar, their flames doubled in the polished stone floor until the whole hall seems to float on fire. Carved granite pillars recede into shadow. Beyond an open outer doorway, monsoon rain falls in a silver sheet. The nobles of Travancore stand packed in ranks, bare-chested in temple fashion, fine mundus and shoulder cloths, gold at their ears and throats catching the lamplight.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The monsoon of 1750, three days after Kottarakkara fell. The king called every noble in the kingdom to Padmanabhaswamy.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Not for war council. Not for treaty.

panels.description: The front ranks from behind and a little above. Nobles in order of importance, composed faces in profile, jewels glinting. In the front rank, one clear gap on the stone where no one stands, a single lamp's reflection lying in it.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Near the front was the place where Padmini would once have stood, stick planted, eyes sharp.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Fever had taken her months before. The gap she left was as visible as any banner.

panels.description: Nagoji at the back of the hall among the lesser officers. He is Ananthan Pillai in temple dress: Kerala topknot with grey at the temples, cream mundu, shoulder cloth over a bare chest, silver chain of office; strong cheekbones, thick curled moustache, clean-shaven chin, small gold ear stud. No coat inside the temple. Two nobles in the rank ahead glance back at him sidelong.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Revathi had not come.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Her absence was noted, weighed, filed away.

panels.description: A temple attendant lowers a great conch from his lips. A herald steps into the lamplight before the assembly, chin raised, voice trained to cut through drums and crowd.

copy.speaker: HERALD
copy.text: Listen and witness.

copy.speaker: HERALD
copy.text: His Highness Sree Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma, Maharaja of Travancore.

copy.speaker: HERALD
copy.text: Victor of Colachel. Breaker of the Eight Houses.

panels.description: Full width, bottom. At the far doorway, Marthanda Varma enters. V13 varma-v1 face, aged: low knot, plain white mundu, bare torso with the sacred thread across his chest, no crown, no jewels, no headwear. He carries a sword flat across both palms, its hilt wrapped in silk, its blade catching the flames. Every head in the hall has turned.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: I had heard him called Varma, called Maharaja, called tiger.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Hearing the whole weight of him spoken aloud inside a temple made the air feel thinner.

panels.description: Low wide shot down the aisle of lamps. Varma walks the length of the mandapa alone, small between the silent ranks, the sword across his palms. At the far end, before the sanctum, a row of temple priests chanting. The chief priest uses the V13 temple-priest face.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The priests' chant was a river of sound. It had flowed here long before any of us were born.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: It would flow long after we were dust.

panels.description: The threshold of the sanctum. Varma from behind, dwarfed. Through the doors, Lord Padmanabha reclining on the great serpent Anantha, seen only in fragments of gold and shadow: a vast shoulder, a resting hand, the many hoods of the serpent rising above. Draw it with reverence. The hoods seem to lean in the flicker of the lamps.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: A thousand eyes, watching the one man who dared to stand before them.

panels.description: Inset, dark. Beneath the flagged floor, a vault in blackness. Heaped coins and old chests catch a single thread of light: Roman gold, Venetian ducats, Dutch guilders, coins of empires long gone.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The true weight of this place was not in the stone. It was under it.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The black gold of pepper, turned into the yellow gold of offerings. Enough to buy the Dutch East India Company three times over.

panels.description: Varma kneeling on the cold stone before the threshold, head bowed. Behind him the nobles are out of focus and utterly still. A lamp in the near foreground, its flame bending.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The silence was absolute. I could hear the hiss of oil in the nearest lamp.

panels.description: Tight, full-width strip. His hands lowering the sword to the stone, point toward the god, the silk-wrapped hilt touching down last.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: It did not clatter. He laid it down the way a father lays down a sleeping child.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Steel touching stone. One soft, final click.

panels.description: Varma still kneeling, face raised toward the sanctum, lit gold from within.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: From this day, I am no longer king of this land.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: I am only the servant of He who lies here.

panels.description: Wide, from the back of the hall over the heads of the nobles. The kneeling figure is small and bright at the far end. His balloons reach all the way back to us.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: All that I have taken, all that I have built, all that I have paid for in blood and exile and broken houses...

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: I give to Him. The kingdom is His. I merely hold it in trust.

panels.description: The priests raise their hands, the chant swelling. In the foreground, an old noble's face, eyes wet, lips moving in prayer.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The pious among them saw a king humbling himself before his god.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Others saw the trap.

panels.description: At the back, beside Nagoji, a minor chief from the northern marches leans to his neighbour, eyes wide, voice kept under the chant. Nagoji does not turn his head.

copy.speaker: CHIEF (whisper)
copy.text: He has given the land to god, so that he can keep it forever.

panels.description: The neighbour's lips twitch but do not smile. The chief goes on.

copy.speaker: CHIEF (whisper)
copy.text: Who can take from a god what a god owns? Not Mysore. Not the Nizam. Not the Dutch.

copy.speaker: CHIEF (whisper)
copy.text: Not even a woman with a legitimate claim.

panels.description: Ramayyan Dalawa near the front, side-on to the sanctum: thin, sharp fine features, receding hair, plain white cloth, a palm-leaf bundle under one arm. He is not watching the king and not watching the god. His eyes move along the bowed rows, lingering on a stiff shoulder here, a lifted chin there.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: He was checking the mortar on this new wall they had built.

panels.description: Nagoji, close, lamplight across half his face, looking from Ramayyan to the kneeling king.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: I understood then.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: He had built walls of stone and armies of men. Now he built a wall of faith, and it was the strongest of them all.

panels.description: Varma rising from his knees. The sword stays where he laid it at the threshold, drinking the lamplight. From the side, a temple attendant steps forward carrying something long and plain. The nobles shift.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: But he was not finished.

panels.description: Inset, tight. A common broom, the kind any sweeper uses, its bristles worn from honest work, passing from the attendant's hands into the king's.

Full width, bottom. Varma sweeping the stone before the sanctum in slow, deliberate strokes, gathering dust, scattered flower petals, ash from a thousand offerings. The nobles in the background frozen.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The murmuring died. I could hear the oil lamps hissing, and the bristles scraping on the stone.

panels.description: Large, top half of the page. High angle down the long pillared corridor that runs around the temple, lamps receding in two long lines. Far down it, one small bare-chested figure with a broom, mid-stroke. Nobles stand at the edges like statues. Past the outer wall, rain on the dark leaves of the serpent grove.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The king who had broken the Dutch, who had shattered the Eight Houses, who had built an army that made Mysore think twice.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Like any temple servant.

panels.description: The whispering chief from page 3, watching the broom go past him. The knowing look has gone out of his face.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: This was not theatre. This was a man who meant what he said.

panels.description: Back before the sanctum. Varma's mundu grey with dust, his hands grey with ash. He hands the broom back to the attendant.
Nagoji's point of view across the hall. Varma has turned to face the assembly, and his eyes have found Nagoji's.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In his gaze, only the weariness of a man who had placed his last piece on the board and could only wait to see if the game was won.

panels.description: Full width, bottom. The priests intone. Row after row of heads going down across the mandapa, the whispering chief's among them. Beyond the bowed king, the sword gleams at the god's threshold.

copy.speaker: PRIESTS
copy.text: Padmanabha Dasa.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Servant of Padmanabha.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The land belonged to god now.

copy.speaker: CAPTION (separate, weighted)
copy.text: And god's servant still held the sword.

panels.description: Wide. A fort courtyard in early evening. Above the gate, the Travancore banner, a silver conch on red, lifting in the wind. Revathi Bayi stands alone on the flagstones looking up at it: deep indigo sari with gold, grey threading her black hair, jasmine in her braid, the tali on its yellow thread, flat-coin necklace, gold armlets, sandalwood line at the hairline. Behind her, in a doorway, Nagoji in uniform: white European-cut coat, red waistcoat, brass buttons, Kerala topknot, silver chain, sword at his hip.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: One week later.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: That banner flew now over all the lands that had once been a dozen kingdoms.

panels.description: Two-shot. She still faces the banner, not him. He has come a few steps into the courtyard.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: She reached Kochi. They gave her a small house. She tends a garden now.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: I am glad she lives.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: Are you?

panels.description: Nagoji, silent, jaw set, the banner's shadow across him. Her next balloon comes in from off-panel and lands on his face.

copy.speaker: REVATHI (off)
copy.text: You could have let her go. During the battle. You were close enough.

copy.speaker: REVATHI (off)
copy.text: She was trying to reach the boats.

panels.description: Revathi turns her head to him at last. No heat in her face, only weariness.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: I did not see her.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: Liar.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: Perhaps.

panels.description: Close on Revathi, looking at him as if seeing him for the first time. Nagoji soft in the background.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: You have made your choice. Completely now. There is no more standing with one foot in each river.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: You are his man. His sword. His builder.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI (off)
copy.text: Yes.

panels.description: Wide two-shot, a long stretch of flagstone between them.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: And I am still hers. Her kinswoman. Her blood. The one who stood beside you in the same hall while you burned her claim.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: Velinadu sent no men against us. You kept your doors closed.

panels.description: Revathi turning away a step, toward the gate, her face in profile against the evening light.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: Closed is not the same as open.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: Silence is not the same as support.

panels.description: She turns back.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: We will not be enemies. Velinadu and Travancore need each other too much for that.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: But we will never be simple. You chose. So did I.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: What did you choose?

panels.description: Tight on Revathi.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: To remember.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: When everyone else forgets what this cost, I will remember. Savitri's face. Her garden in Kochi. The laugh she will never laugh again.

panels.description: Full width, bottom. Revathi walking out through the gate into the low gold evening, small, not looking back. Nagoji in the near foreground, still, the banner above them both. Her last balloons trail back to him.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: Someone has to carry that weight. It will not be you. It will not be him.

copy.speaker: REVATHI
copy.text: So it will be me.

panels.description: Wide. Mavelikkara, 1753. A pavilion table. A VOC commissioner in a dark formal coat and white cravat signs with a quill; Dutch soldiers in blue coats stand at the back. Across the table, Ramayyan watches the pen, palm-leaf bundle at his elbow.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The Great Offering did what accounts and cannons could not. It silenced the threats inside the house.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Three years later the Dutch came back to Mavelikkara. This time they did not just bow. They signed.

panels.description: Night. A fort rampart, the stone still wet. Varma alone at the parapet, staring out at nothing: aged varma-v1 face, low knot, plain white mundu, a plain shoulder cloth, no jewels. Nagoji in uniform coming along the wall walk toward him.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: But the final cost of that peace was not written in ink.

panels.description: Varma, not turning, speaking to the dark.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: The Nizam sent an envoy last month. Mysore's man was here before that.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: The British build at Madras as if they mean to stay forever. And the Dutch, even now, count their losses and plan their next move.

panels.description: He turns to face Nagoji.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: This is what I was always building toward. Not conquering for glory. Consolidating for survival.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: A kingdom strong enough that when they come, any of them, all of them, they will find more than pepper and prayers.

panels.description: Nagoji, close, his face unreadable.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: And the cost?

panels.description: Varma, looking back out over the dark.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: The cost is that men like Savitri's kinsman die in rooms they cannot leave.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: That women like her tend gardens in foreign cities and curse my name.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: That Revathi looks at me like I am the disease I claimed to cure.

panels.description: Tight on his hands gripping the parapet, knuckles pale against the wet stone.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: Do you think I do not feel it? Do you think I do not wake in the night and hear them?

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: Every name. Every claim I denied. Every law I bent or broke.

panels.description: Varma's face, close, his voice cracking. Behind him, bleeding into the panel edge like a stain rather than a clean flashback frame: a sunlit courtyard years ago, a young noblewoman with her head thrown back in laughter.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: I remember her laugh. From when we were young.

panels.description: He does not look at Nagoji.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: And I remember the moment, in that tent, when I looked in her eyes and saw that she would never laugh again.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: I did that. For this.

panels.description: Full width, bottom. Wide over the rampart: the king's arm opening out toward the dark kingdom below, the lamps of forts on the far hills, the pale line of a road, the ordered cookfires of an army camp. Two small figures on the wall.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: For this.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: I had no comfort to offer.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Some wounds are the price of building. Some prices are too high to name, but too necessary not to pay.

panels.description: Wide. Evening, a quiet corner of Udayagiri Fort. A small chapel of local stone with a simple wooden cross above its door. Through the open door: De Lannoy, tall, grey-haired, in his white Travancore coat, kneeling in the front pew with his head bowed; Father Duarte at a small altar, hands raised, white-haired now, plain black cassock with a small cross, no collar tab. Nagoji in uniform waits outside by the doorpost.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Udayagiri Fort. The treaty was signed, and the Dutch had sailed away with their diminished pride.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Latin words that meant nothing to me, and everything to the man who listened.

panels.description: De Lannoy stepping out into the evening light, a peace in his face rarely seen in the war halls.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: Pillai. You do not usually visit this part of the fort.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: I do not usually find two Europeans praying to their god in a kingdom that just surrendered itself to ours.

panels.description: Duarte in the doorway behind him. The scholar's stoop, the ink-stained fingers, the grey tired eyes under white hair.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: His eyes still carried the grey tiredness I remembered from the dungeon. Only now it looked less like guilt and more like acceptance.

copy.speaker: DUARTE
copy.text: The Maharaja has been generous. He permits us this small space. We ask nothing of him but the right to serve.

panels.description: De Lannoy, a glance back at the pew he left.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: And to pray. A man needs something beyond walls and accounts.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: Otherwise the walls become a prison and the accounts become chains.

panels.description: The three of them together in the low evening light between the chapel door and the fort wall.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: A Maratha cavalryman, a Dutch artillerist, a Portuguese priest. Twenty years ago our peoples were killing each other across three continents.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: The banner does not ask where we came from. Only where we stand now.

panels.description: Duarte steps forward. His right hand, callused and ink-stained, rises and stops in the air between them. Hold it. Nagoji watching the hand.
The hand completes the motion: a sign of the cross in Nagoji's direction, quick but deliberate.

copy.speaker: DUARTE
copy.text: I do not do this to convert you. It is the only blessing I know how to give.

copy.speaker: DUARTE
copy.text: And you have earned a blessing, Ananthan Pillai. Whatever you believe.

panels.description: A lighter beat. De Lannoy half-smiling; Duarte with the ghost of a smile.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: Even Ramayyan visited once. He spent the whole time examining the stonework.

copy.speaker: DUARTE
copy.text: He said the mortar was acceptable. High praise, from him.

panels.description: De Lannoy looking down at the flagstones of the chapel floor. Quiet.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: When I die, I have asked to be buried here. In this fort I helped design. Under a stone that says I served Travancore.

copy.speaker: DUARTE
copy.text: And I will say the words over you. If God grants me the years.

panels.description: Full width, bottom. De Lannoy clasps Nagoji's arm. Duarte beside them. The fort wall behind, the evening sky above it.

copy.speaker: DE LANNOY
copy.text: We are all servants now. It is a strange household. But it holds.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The kingdom had absorbed us all. And somehow, in the absorbing, it had made us more than we had been alone.

panels.description: Wide. A star-fort rampart at dusk, monsoon clouds building over the sea. Nagoji old now, later-life sheet: grey-streaked hair in a topknot, white mundu with a gold border, the same thick moustache and clean-shaven chin, small gold ear stud, leaning on the parapet. Beside him a young Travancore officer in a white European-cut coat and red waistcoat.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Years later, when my joints ached with old battles.

copy.speaker: OFFICER
copy.text: What was Travancore like, before it was Travancore?

panels.description: Inset. Remembered: the map on the war-hall table, the coast divided into many coloured territories.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Red for Mysore. Black for the Nizam. Brown for Arcot. Blue for the Europeans.

panels.description: Nagoji, turned toward the young man.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: It was smaller. And more divided. And more free, in some ways.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: And more vulnerable.

copy.speaker: OFFICER
copy.text: Do you miss it?

panels.description: Large panel. What the wall looks down on: musketeers drilling by volley in the yard below, a shore battery trained on the sea, a line of star forts along the coast, horsemen riding through the surf without flinching, Marakkar ships flying the king's conch flag beside their own.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: When I first washed ashore, the king borrowed lancers from Madurai and begged muskets from English factors. His horses feared the sand.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Now there were fifty thousand men under arms. All of it built in twenty years. All of it paid for in pepper and blood.

panels.description: Nagoji, close, old eyes on the young man.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: I miss what it cost.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: He did not understand. He had been born into the kingdom we built.

panels.description: Faded, bleeding in from the panel edge like old ink: the Goa interrogation room from Chapter 1. Young Nagoji in captivity rags, bound to the stool, hands bandaged; the younger Duarte, dark-haired, standing before him.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI (faded)
copy.text: He seems to favour whoever has the better powder.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: That young man had been wrong. Belief had turned out to matter more than anything.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Just not the kind the priest was selling.

panels.description: Memory, lamplit. Revathi's western verandah on a wet night, years back: Revathi in indigo with jasmine and the tali, turning away toward a small girl running on the wet stone, one hand raised to scold. Nagoji behind her in mundu and shoulder cloth, mouth closed.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: One night on her western verandah, I almost told her I would lay down my marches if she asked. The words sat on my tongue like a loaded musket.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Perhaps that mercy was hers, not mine.

panels.description: Wide, split down the middle, the same rain falling across both halves. Left: a small garden in Kochi, Savitri old and in white, among her plants. Right: a Velinadu courtyard, Revathi grey-haired on the verandah, children running laughing through the wet corridors.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The monsoon came that year, as it always did.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In Kochi, an old woman tended her garden. In Velinadu, another remembered, while my grandchildren ran through the rain.

panels.description: Large, bottom half of the page. Nagoji alone on the fort wall in the rain, face lifted to it, eyes closed. Beyond and below him the whole kingdom under the same rain: forts, roads, fields, the grey sea.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: That was the price. That was always the price.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Some things do not wash.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Some things we carry.

copy.speaker: CAPTION (separate, weighted)
copy.text: For as long as we live, and in the stories that outlast us.
